notes: greedy_fast, not raw generate_greedy, is the baseline: generate_lookup's prefill computes last-position logits only, evaluated per chunk, which is already cheaper than generate_greedy's single all-position forward. greedy_fast prefills exactly like generate_lookup (same chunking, same last-position-only logits, same make_trimmable_cache) so the comparison isolates drafting, not the prefill scheme (controller ruling, 2026-09-26).

prefill_s is each method's OWN prefill wall time: greedy_fast returns its own (from the same _lookup_prefill call it decodes from), and generate_lookup returns its own via stats['prefill_s']. decode_s = (that call's own end-to-end wall time) - (that same call's own prefill_s); on a very fast, very short generation this can occasionally go slightly negative from timing noise, in which case decode_s is floored rather than reported as infinite tok/s. Earlier drafts of this script subtracted greedy_fast's prefill_s from generate_lookup's total (a different cache slack, n_draft+1 vs greedy_fast's 64) -- fixed per S4 review round 1, since that over-corrected generate_lookup's decode_s in its own favour on exactly the long-prefix workload the 1.1x keep decision is gated on.

identical (vs greedy_fast, not generate_greedy) < 1 is hypothesized to come from bf16 exact logit near-ties broken differently between greedy_fast's single-token decode steps and generate_lookup's batched-verify steps (same hypothesis as results/dflash.json); first_divergence records where, in tokens.

Session prefixes are the last up-to-8192 tokens of the session's tokenized transcript, ending right before the start of the *last* assistant turn (replay.session tokenize's assistant mask) -- the context an agent had just before deciding what to write next, which is where prompt-lookup drafting is expected to pay off most.

Settings differ per target (see the top-level `settings` key). resident sweeps g=4/n=3 fixed, g=4/n=3 adaptive, g=4/n=7 fixed: results/lookup_acceptance.json (commit 22f84f1) re-ran S2's offline simulation against S1's MEASURED verify costs (not the earlier provisional linear model) and predicts g=4/n=3 fixed as resident's best expected speedup (1.483x) and g=4/n=3 adaptive close behind (1.478x) -- both ahead of g=4/n=7 fixed (1.297x, kept here only as the comparison point against the earlier settings). streaming is restricted to short drafts (verify-block length <= 4 tokens: g=4/n=3 fixed, g=4/n=3 adaptive, g=4/n=2 fixed), dropping the n=7/n=15 settings resident uses, because results/dflash_diag.json measured a streaming verify-cost cliff, not a curve: median verify_ms was 37.8@block=1, 61.9@block=4, then 212.0@block=6 and 574.1@block=16. A block of drafted tokens > 4 can route more experts/token than the 32-slot expert cache holds at once, forcing StreamingSwitchGLU into multiple masked passes per layer; the same measured-cost sweep in results/lookup_acceptance.json confirms it directly -- streaming g=4/n=7 fixed predicts 0.692x (slower than no drafting at all), vs 1.697x for g=4/n=3 fixed (S1 follow-up, 2026-09-26).
Timings may include noise from concurrent human activity on the machine.
Single run per setting; no repeats.
